text: Reading Four · Allen & Shaw, in Luiselli (ed.), 2011 Naturalistic Teaching Overview: what we know Early behavioral treatments for individuals with autism used basic principles of learning to create highly effective teaching interactions. Their success was largely a result of highly structured training procedures, developed specifically to maximize learning potential: distractions were minimized, prompts were delivered in a precise sequence, practices were massed, and consequences were delivered in a reliable, immediate, and frequent manner. These tightly controlled procedures, known as discrete trial training, have been found to be quite effective at teaching new and complex skills, and led to impressive gains in language, social, and adaptive skills for many individuals with autism. Unfortunately, these highly structured approaches were not without problems. Of significant concern was the fact that many newly acquired skills would be exhibited in the highly structured learning environment but not in the less structured natural environment. The skills learned in controlled training settings did not automatically transfer, or generalize, to other important settings (regular classroom, playground), other important people (peers, parents), or other important tasks (play, daily living tasks). For example, a child who had learned to say "truck" when presented with a picture of a truck in a tightly controlled treatment setting would not necessarily say "truck" when he wanted access to his toy truck at home. Over recent years, naturalistic teaching has emerged as a way to address this problem with generalization. Naturalistic teaching promotes generalization of skills to the natural or everyday settings where those skills are required. Recent reviews have found that research support for this approach is extensive (see Allen & Cowen, 2008). Naturalistic procedures have been found to enhance the generalization of language, social, and play skills, and in direct comparisons with more structured approaches have, in many situations, been found to produce better generalization of important skills to the natural environment. In addition, because naturalistic procedures occur within the context of everyday life and activities, they can help make learning more fun and in many cases increase a child's willingness to participate in teaching interactions. Getting started: principles and applications To understand the basic principles of naturalistic teaching, a distinction must be made between two behavioral processes: discrimination and generalization. Discrimination.  When an individual exhibits the correct or desired response under certain stimulus conditions and not others, the individual is said to have discriminated. An individual who selects a truck when asked to select the truck from a choice of truck, cup and shoe has discriminated between different choices. Generalization.  Generalization occurs when that same correct or desired response occurs under similar but untrained stimulus conditions. The individual who can select the truck when the truck looks different — different size, color, or function — from that used during training has demonstrated generalization, as has an individual who responds correctly when the teacher or the setting is different. Discrimination training can be a critical part of learning, because sometimes it is very important that an individual exhibit certain responses under very specific conditions and only those conditions. For example, it is important that individuals learn "stranger danger" and not to get in the car with anyone other than a parent or guardian — which requires that "coming when called" does  not  generalize to every adult who is calling. Likewise, individuals must learn that not all four-legged animals are dogs, not all liquids are juice, not all coins are quarters, and not all buses will arrive downtown. Discrimination is problematic, however, when it leads to an individual being unable to perform certain responses under many different yet important conditions. An individual must learn to ask for help not just from the teacher but also from a boss, a parent, or a peer; to identify a jacket on the coat rack as well as in a picture; to count coins at the store as well as at school; to recite his or her address to a cab driver as well as a parent. When individuals do not generalize important language, social, and play skills from the training environment to everyday life, difficulties in adaptive functioning may result. Guidelines for implementation There is no single or gold standard naturalistic teaching procedure. Various approaches can be found under a number of different names, including incidental teaching, natural language paradigm, behavioral chain interruption, script fading, and milieu teaching. The following guidelines represent an integration of the most distinguishing characteristics of these procedures. Teach responses that will likely create contact with natural reinforcers Generalization is enhanced when an individual is taught a response for which the natural consequence is a reinforcer. Natural consequences are those that would occur naturally, without needing to be programmed by the teacher: a natural consequence to a request for a "truck" is to hand the individual a truck. The use of praise, hugs, or even candy as a consequence would not be a natural consequence of a request for a truck, and these arbitrary consequences would require specific programming by the teacher — and responding may then be limited to conditions where the teacher has arranged for that arbitrary reinforcement. Zach and Mrs. Cole Mrs. Cole has observed that Zach loves playing with cars and trucks during free play, and decides to target Zach's expressive language using the natural reinforcers available. When Zach shows interest, he is required to request to play with the cars and trucks and to elaborate by describing features of the ones he wants first ("Yes, Zach, you may play with the cars and trucks. Which color cars and trucks would you like?" or "How many would you like?"). She hands him a few and, once he is engaged, imposes the same expectations before Zach can access more or different kinds — request plus elaboration. Allow an individual's interests to direct and pace teaching Given the emphasis on natural reinforcers, there will be times when teaching cannot occur because an individual — through illness, fatigue, satiation — is not interested in the current activities or materials. Under highly structured conditions, a teacher might try to overcome this disinterest by introducing arbitrary reinforcers. However, because naturalistic teaching relies on natural reinforcers, teaching is not forced when interest has waned. During free time, Mrs. Cole had planned to work with Zach on sharing and play sequences with cars and trucks, but today Zach followed several children to the kitchen area, where he seems interested in setting the table with plastic dishes, cups, and food. Mrs. Cole follows Zach to the kitchen, takes several plates and pieces of food, holds them within view, and waits for Zach to request them; when he does, she asks him to elaborate the colors, sizes, and categories (fruits or vegetables) he wants and then hands them to him. Later, Zach loses interest in the kitchen and begins pacing the room; although she had hoped to work on turn taking, she recognizes that because his interest is currently low, naturalistic teaching is not appropriate at this time. Embed teaching within the activities of everyday life Generalization is enhanced when training conditions are diverse and loosely structured. The goal is for the individual to be unable to tell where or when training is occurring, so that trained responses occur everywhere and with everyone. By embedding teaching within the activities of everyday life, diversity is increased by the inclusion of multiple "teachers" — paraeducators, parents, peers — across multiple settings (on the playground, in the hallways, in the backyard at home, during a bath, at the mall) and at various times throughout the day. Mrs. Cole has observed that Zach loves playing on swings and slides, and requires him to request to go outside and to elaborate by describing which activity he wants first. She has recruited Zach's parents and daycare providers to do the same, and several peers to act as peer tutors: when Zach is engaged with cars and trucks, she prompts a peer to arrive with additional highly preferred cars, which the peer shares contingent upon Zach's appropriate request. At home, Zach's parents make cars, puzzles, and computers accessible only after appropriate requests and elaborations, working from a list of the elaborations being targeted at school; they also model pushing the cars, making car sounds, and turn taking, and arrange play dates with a selected peer who brings preferred snacks and puzzles that Zach can access by asking what is in his backpack. Back at school, Mrs. Cole occasionally sends Zach on an errand to the office, where the secretary dispenses information only after Zach queries for it and keeps treats in one of three tins, so Zach must ask where they are, request access, and elaborate on the color, size, or number he would like. Incorporate prompts that can be transported to new situations Prompts are most often thought of as teaching methods that help promote learning. However, generalization can also be enhanced by including prompts within one training situation that can easily be transported to new situations. Individuals with autism often do not initiate social-communicative interactions in any setting, so prompting is often required. The  mand-model  procedure allows a teacher to initiate an interaction by telling the child what is required and then modeling the appropriate response: Mrs. Cole might say, "What do you want?" and immediately model, "Say, 'I want a car.'" She might also introduce a  time-delay  procedure, gradually increasing the time between her request and her model, giving Zach a chance to respond but helping him before he gets frustrated or loses interest. She could also use a  script-fading  procedure in which visual or auditory cues are provided in the natural setting: to teach Zach to approach a group at recess and request a turn on a swing, she teaches him to follow a written script, initially prompting and reinforcing script following in a tightly controlled setting, and eventually letting him take the script to recess on a small laminated card in his back pocket, where another teacher prompts him to look at and follow the script as needed. Adaptations and modifications Restrict access One of the common obstacles to naturalistic teaching is that opportunities are lost because individuals have unlimited or only slightly restricted access to the things that interest them most. With some increased restrictions and a touch of creativity, many additional opportunities can be created. Mrs. Cole has arranged the classroom so that some of Zach's most preferred activities and objects are visible but not easily accessed: his favorite cars and puzzles are on top of a cabinet that only adults can reach. When he arrives each day his dessert and drink are removed from his lunch, so he must initiate additional requests to access them; his coat and boots are moved, so after a request to go outside he is prompted to ask a classroom aide or peer tutor for their location. At home, computer games are locked in a cabinet and the best DVD is always in a novel location, requiring queries and social exchanges with parents and siblings. Interrupt chains Although much of naturalistic teaching occurs at the beginning of potential interactions, when motivation is high, there are times when it can occur in the middle of an activity sequence. Behavior chain interruption involves an interruption of the chain or flow of purposeful behavior in the midst of a familiar routine. Zach's parents typically require him to request to play a computer game, but they have also purchased a timer that limits his time; when the time elapses, a 60-second countdown warns Zach of impending shutdown, his play is interrupted, and he must find his parents and initiate a request for more time. His parents have also taught him to make his own peanut-butter-and-jelly sandwich; once mastered, they intentionally arrange for him to periodically discover that there is only one piece of bread or a very small amount of jelly, so that solving the problem requires interrupting his activities and asking for help. Keys to remember Naturalistic teaching promotes generalization of skills to settings where those skills are required. To find good naturalistic teaching opportunities, follow the individual's interests and activities. Learning does not need to occur just in the classroom or in tightly controlled, distraction-free environments. Look for opportunities to teach within the context of everyday events with everyday people. Not all skills can be learned through naturalistic teaching. Some new or complex skills may be better learned in a more controlled setting before taking that skill into the natural setting.
